issues.legal_issue: The statutory allocation of criminal cases between a local village tribunal and ordinary criminal courts was not discriminatory merely because the two forums followed different procedures.
material_facts: The statute gave the village tribunal jurisdiction over specified offences, subject to other provisions of the statute.
A case cognizable by the village tribunal could not ordinarily be taken cognizance of by another court unless an authorized judicial officer ordered otherwise.
Other provisions allowed cases to be transferred to the village tribunal, withdrawn from it, or removed from its jurisdiction in specified circumstances.
The village tribunal was not bound to follow the ordinary rules of evidence and procedure.
issues.conclusion: The statutory scheme was not discriminatory and did not infringe the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, the challenged scheme was not discriminatory because, read as a whole, it did not leave a complainant free to choose between the village tribunal and an ordinary criminal court. Section 62, which made the tribunal’s jurisdiction concurrent, was subject to the rest of the Act, including section 68, which generally reserved cognizance of tribunal cases to that tribunal unless an authorized order provided otherwise. Sections 69, 70 and 73 provided for transfer, withdrawal, and intervention in cases of miscarriage or apprehended miscarriage of justice; these provisions explained the reference to concurrent jurisdiction. The different procedure under section 60 therefore did not create the asserted choice of forums.

predicates.case_cognizable_by_village_tribunal: The proceeding concerned an offence assigned by law to a village tribunal for trial.
predicates.ordinary_court_cognizance_requires_autho: The law generally prevented an ordinary court from taking cognizance of a case assigned to the village tribunal unless an authorized judicial officer ordered otherwise.
predicates.exceptional_transfer_or_withdrawal_is_pr: The law allowed an authorized judicial officer to transfer a case, withdraw it from the village tribunal, or intervene when justice might miscarry.

issues.definition: When a case is assigned to a village tribunal, ordinary-court cognizance is controlled by an authorized order, and the law provides for exceptional transfers or withdrawals, the forum scheme is not discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge based on alleged noncompliance with the village tribunal’s decision-recording rules fails where the decision and any dissent were recorded as required and no breach is shown.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the village tribunal’s compliance with rules governing its decisions.
The full-bench decision was signed by its members, and the dissenting members’ minute was recorded under their signatures.
No material was presented showing that the relevant rules had been violated.
issues.conclusion: The procedural challenge was rejected because the stated recording requirements were fulfilled and no violation of the rules was shown.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 60(2) of the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules, 1949 required the full-bench decision to be signed by its members and a dissenting minute to be recorded under the dissenting members’ signatures. The Court found those requirements fulfilled and found no material establishing a violation of rules 60 or 61.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_village_tribunal and decision_signed_by_members and dissent_recorded_under_dissenters_signatures and no_material_shows_rule_breach

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_village_tribunal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning a criminal decision made by a village tribunal.
predicates.decision_signed_by_members: The members who made the full-bench decision signed it.
predicates.dissent_recorded_under_dissenters_signat: The dissenting members’ minute was recorded under their signatures.
predicates.no_material_shows_rule_breach: The challenger presented no material showing that the applicable decision-recording rules had been violated.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal from a village tribunal, the procedural challenge is rejected when the decision and any dissent were recorded as required and no rule breach is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand where the prosecution evidence does not identify the accused as participants and the accused’s statement, standing alone, does not establish guilt.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses identified certain participants but did not identify the two accused whose convictions were challenged.
The accused’s statement that he had removed crops from his own field, considered by itself, was not an admission of guilt.
No other evidence supported those two convictions.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the two accused were set aside, and they were discharged from bail.
issues.legal_principle: A conviction must have an evidentiary basis implicating the accused; an accused’s statement that, standing alone, is not an admission of guilt cannot supply that basis. The Court exercised its supervisory power under Article 227 in the appeal to set aside convictions that were manifestly erroneous on the face of the record.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and prosecution_witnesses_do_not_identify_accused and no_other_evidence_implicates_accused and accused_statement_alone_is_not_admission

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_do_not_identify_ac: The prosecution witnesses described participants but did not identify the accused as among them.
predicates.no_other_evidence_implicates_accused: No other evidence in the record connected the accused to the offence.
predicates.accused_statement_alone_is_not_admission: The accused made a statement which, considered by itself, did not amount to an admission of guilt.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a criminal conviction, the conviction is set aside when prosecution witnesses do not identify the accused, no other evidence implicates the accused, and the accused’s statement alone is not an admission.

issues.legal_issue: A supported criminal conviction may be maintained while a short custodial sentence is replaced with a fine when imprisonment would serve no useful purpose.
material_facts: Prosecution witnesses identified the accused as a participant in removing the crops.
The Court considered that accused’s conviction to be rightly made.
The sentence was a short period of imprisonment, and the Court found no useful purpose would be served by sending the accused to jail for that period.
issues.conclusion: The conviction was maintained, but the sentence was reduced to a fine, with imprisonment in default as directed by the village tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the conviction as supported by the evidence but exercised its appellate power to modify the sentence because it considered that the short custodial term would serve no useful purpose. No specific earlier case or statutory sentencing provision was cited for this sentencing modification.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and evidence_supports_conviction and custodial_sentence_is_short and imprisonment_would_serve_no_useful_purpose

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.evidence_supports_conviction: The evidence identified the accused as a participant in the offence.
predicates.custodial_sentence_is_short: The sentence imposed was a short term of imprisonment.
predicates.imprisonment_would_serve_no_useful_purpo: The Court considered that serving the short custodial term would serve no useful purpose.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a supported criminal conviction, a short custodial sentence is replaced with a fine when imprisonment would serve no useful purpose.
